Russia-linked hackers used the volunteer-run Yggdrasil network to conceal communications during an attack on a Ukrainian grain logistics company, marking the first documented use of the technology by a state-linked hacking group, cybersecurity firm ESET said on Thursday.
The attack culminated in the destruction of data at the company, which forms part of Ukraine’s vital agricultural export sector. Agriculture accounted for roughly a fifth of Ukraine’s economy and nearly half its exports before the war, according to research estimates.
ESET traced the July 2025 intrusion to a phishing email sent as part of an ongoing campaign targeting logistics firms, grain companies and port terminals in Ukraine, researcher Anton Cherepanov said.
The attackers installed software that allowed them to remotely control infected computers, browse files, take screenshots and steal documents. The software communicated through a server hidden inside Yggdrasil, an experimental volunteer-run network with no central owner.
“Because it’s a mesh network, it’s harder to detect,” Cherepanov said. ESET said it had not previously observed state-linked attacks using the network.
After gaining administrator privileges, the attackers activated a data-wiping tool that deleted data from affected computers, Cherepanov said. The tool used was SDelete, a legitimate Microsoft utility designed to permanently erase files.
“They abused this legitimate tool,” he said.
“SDelete is a legitimate, publicly available administrative utility that IT professionals use to securely delete data. Like many legitimate tools, it can be misused by malicious actors who have already gained access to a network,” a Microsoft spokesperson told Reuters in an email.
ESET said it could not determine what the affected systems were used for and could not confirm whether the attack disrupted grain operations.
The initial intrusion was carried out by a Russia-linked hacking group known as UAC-0099, which ESET said specializes in gaining access to networks. The subsequent data destruction bore the hallmarks of Sandworm, a hacking group widely linked to Russian military intelligence and previously blamed for cyberattacks on Ukrainian and Polish power infrastructure.
ESET assessed that UAC-0099 successfully gained access and handed it to Sandworm, but said it could not determine which group operated the previously unseen backdoor used between the breach and the data destruction.
The firm declined to identify the victim company.
(Reporting by Leo Marchandon in Gdansk; editing by Matt Scuffham and Joyjeet Das)

Romanian President Nicusor Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO’s eastern flank on Friday, after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off the Romanian Black Sea coast, killing at least one sailor with three still missing.
Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above the waves as it sank. Emergency vessels were searching the surrounding waters for survivors in choppy seas and high wind.
Romania’s naval authority said the Comoros-flagged Khoryv, with a crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors, had sent a distress signal 13 nautical miles off Romania’s port of Constanta, just beyond Romanian territorial waters. Nine sailors were rescued from the water, three were missing and one body was recovered.
Read more: Russia Drones Are Already Killing People Within EU Territory
The past two weeks have seen a sudden surge in deadly attacks on commercial ships off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and some 30 sailors reported dead or missing.
“It is part of Russia’s escalation process in its war in Ukraine,” President Dan told reporters, later saying the ship had been hit by a drone.
NATO said on Tuesday it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea. The alliance has not specified what capabilities would be sent. On Saturday, Romanian jetsshot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters.
The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea.
The canal has become the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world’s biggest grain and food oil exporters, which has relied on Danube River ports and Romanian territorial watersas Russia has attacked Ukraine’s own Black Sea ports.
Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
(Reporting by Luiza Ilie; editing by Peter Graff)

Storm Austen knocked out electricity to almost 300,000 customers in western France on Friday as hurricane-force winds battered the region, disrupting roads, railways and other transport links.
Brittany was hardest hit, with almost 150,000 customers without power, according to distributor Enedis. Amber weather alerts are in place across northwest Spain and France, and the western half of Germany. One region in northern Germany near the Harz Mountains is under a red alert for high winds.
Airports on Jersey and Guernsey were closed. Cancellations and delays are mounting at Paris airports, according to data from Flight tracking site Flightradar24.
Read more: Storm Austen Will Be Stronger Than Forecast Along UK Coasts
Austen is the first named storm this autumn and it’s also sending power prices in France and Germany tumbling. A surge in wind generation is flooding grids with cheap electricity, offering some relief to markets that have been grappling with the highest natural gas prices since the 2022 energy crisis.
In Germany, Europe’s biggest power market, wind generation is poised to set a new output record on Friday and could come close to meeting all the nation’s needs on Sunday, although curtailment and must-run generation may limit actual output. Kpler SA forecasts that power prices will drop to €29 a megawatt-hour on Saturday and near zero on Sunday, the lowest since April.
French prices are also forecast to plunge, falling to about €17 on Sunday, the lowest since June. The burst of wind generation reduces the need for more expensive gas-fired plants, which often set prices when renewable output is low.
Austen swept through the English Channel on Friday, lashing both coasts of France and England with heavy rain. Gusts as high as 140 kilometers per hour (87 miles) are expected in some French coastal areas, equivalent to a Category 1 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson scale, according to Météo-France.
Enedis has mobilized more than 2,000 personnel since Wednesday, with several hundred additional technicians being sent to the hardest-hit areas as part of its rapid response force. In Normandy, cuts affected 88,800 customers, 49,600 in Pays de la Loire and almost 8,000 in Hauts-de-France, Enedis said.
The storm also disrupted transport across northern and western France. Several roads and train lines around Paris and in Normandy, Brittany and Hauts-de-France were interrupted, Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said on X.
In the UK, airports on the Channel Islands of Jersey, Guernsey and Alderney were closed until Friday afternoon. About 20,000 people lost power in southwest England, according to National Grid.
The UK day-ahead power price for Saturday settled at £37 per megawatt-hour, less than half of the average so far this year according to data from Epex Spot.
A second storm, named Boelo, is set to follow this weekend, taking a more northerly route across Northern Ireland, Scotland and northern England, according to the UK Met Office. Boelo could bring winds of as much as 129 kilometers an hour to coastal areas along with heavy rain. The UK has issued amber weather warnings for that storm starting Saturday.
The storm patterns could push wind speeds in Europe’s key power markets to 31% above the 10-year average through Nov. 4, helping to offset increased heating demand and weaker solar generation, BloombergNEF said in a note.

New York’s City Council voted to ban horse-drawn carriages, ending a Central Park tourist staple dating to the 19th century after years of debate over the horses’ place on city streets.
The Council voted 40 to 7 to pass the bill Thursday, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani is expected to sign. Two members abstained. The ban takes effect June 1, 2028, and prohibits the sale of horses for slaughter or their transfer to other carriage companies.
The vote ends a fight that has simmered for more than a decade, pitting the city’s roughly 150 carriage drivers and their union against animal-rights advocates and drawing in politicians and celebrities on both sides. Supporters see the clip-clop of hooves through Central Park as part of New York’s appeal, romanticized in film and television; critics say horse-drawn carriages are an anachronism ill-suited to the city’s traffic, pollution and crowded streets.
As the council prepared to vote, President Donald Trump weighed in, criticizing the city’s lawmakers.
“The Horse-drawn Carriage in New York City is a quintessential New York experience,” Trump, who was born in New York, wrote in a social media post. “So sad that, for political reasons, we will see it go!”
The legislation includes a promise to construct a plan by April 1, 2027, for aiding carriage drivers in finding new jobs after the ban takes effect. That plan could include financial compensation for carriage drivers and owners, but doesn’t guarantee it.
Sixty-eight horse cabs are currently licensed to operate in Central Park, under a system that’s capped the number of carriages since the second World War. In addition to the drivers, the industry has more than 180 horses, according to industry spokesperson Christina Hansen.
Carriage industry employees and horse and stable owners say the bill doesn’t go far enough in providing for their financial futures.
“This bill is a train wreck of constitutional and due process violations,” John Samuelsen, president of the Transport Workers Union International, which represents the carriage drivers, said in a statement. “It offers nothing concrete for blue-collar drivers and carriage owners who will be financially crushed, stripped of their jobs, their licenses, expensive city-issued medallions, small businesses, and way of life.”
The union has vowed to seek a temporary restraining order after Mamdani signs the bill.
“We will see them in court,” said Alexander Kemp, administrative vice president for a New York chapter of the union. “This fight is not over.”
The carriages have long faced opposition from animal rights activists who argue that forcing the horses to work in urban conditions damages their long-term health and is unsafe.
“It’s the end of the road for a vile industry that has forced horses to haul heavy carriages through chaotic traffic and punishing weather until they collapsed and died,” said Ashley Byrne, director of animal-rights organization People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals.
The issue came to the forefront of city politics when former Mayor Bill de Blasio pledged to shut down the industry on his first day in office, while he was running for mayor in 2013. His plan ultimately failed, despite repeated attempts.

Taiwan shut its $5 trillion stock market, schools and offices on Friday as Typhoon Champi barreled toward the island, bringing heavy rain and damaging winds that disrupted flights.
Champi was packing top sustained winds of 155 kilometers (96 miles) an hour, equivalent to a Category 2 hurricane, according to the island’s weather agency, after weakening over the past 24 hours from super typhoon strength. The storm was around 260 kilometers southeast of Taipei’s Taoyuan International Airport as of 2:30 p.m. Friday local time, the bureau added.
Most of Taiwan’s cities and counties shut offices and schools for safety on Friday, while the storm had already killed one person and injured 171, according to government statements. More than 950 international and domestic flights were canceled on Friday, along with some train services.
Read more: Taiwan Halts Stock Trade, Shuts Schools as Typhoon Champi Nears
Taiwan’s stock exchange, the fifth-largest globally, will also be closed Monday for a holiday, giving the island an additional trading gap compared with other markets in the region. The tech-heavy exchange, along with those in South Korea and Japan, has sold off recently as investors track earnings from global tech giants.
Cooler ocean waters and increasing wind shear will steadily shave some intensity from Champi, but it remains a very large cyclone with an expansive wind field, according to the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center. The storm is forecast to pass just east of Taipei early Saturday before curving northeast along mainland China’s east coast on its way toward Japan’s Kyushu.
“The risks that matter now are rain and the size of the wind field,” said James Caron, director of meteorological operations for North America and Asia at Atmospheric G2. “The 185-miles-per-hour peak is behind us.”
Champi achieved super typhoon strength earlier in the week, making it the 10th to reach that level in the northwest Pacific Ocean this season. That’s double the long-term average and just shy of a record 13 during 2015’s El Niño, according to the Hong Kong Observatory. Storms tend to form farther east during the climate phenomenon, giving them more time to accumulate energy over warm, open waters as they churn toward land.

A class-action lawsuit has been filed in an Australian court against Meta Platforms’ Facebook and Instagram that alleges the social media platforms exposed children to harmful content and kept them addicted through algorithms.
The lawsuit, filed in the Federal Court, Australia’s second-highest, by law firm MinterEllison this month could be the first in Australia to blame social media for harming its users, particularly children and teenagers.
- The class-action suit has been filed on behalf of eight plaintiffs, who allege they were harmed by Meta while they were under the age of 18, and are seeking compensation.
- “We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously,” a Meta spokesperson said by email.
- In a suppression order on Monday, the court prohibited the reporting of any information which could reveal the identity of the applicants, and the statement of claim.
- The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and Big Tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
- Meta in August agreed to pay $18 billion to settle with nearly all US states to resolve claims it designed social media to addict children.

E-bikes now rival motorcycles for speed. State and city laws haven’t caught up.
Electric bikes and electric scooters parked on a street in Columbus, Ohio. Lawmakers in Ohio and many other states have enacted or are considering tougher regulations for e-bikes and e-scooters as their popularity – and safety concerns – grow. (Photo by Megan Henry/Ohio Capital Journal).
Earlier this month, a 50-year-old man riding his personal electric scooter in Washington, D.C., was killed when he collided with a woman on a rideshare scooter.
In June, a 12-year-old Massachusetts girl died after her electric scooter slammed into a school bus in a suburb of Boston.
And in April, an Atlanta woman riding an electric bike was killed when she hit a curb and was thrown headfirst into a wall.
A string of high-profile deaths and injuries involving electric scooters and bikes is spurring states and cities across the country to crack down on them. As technology improves, e-scooters and e-bikes capable of motorcycle-like speeds have become cheaper and more popular. Some models — and the ability to modify them with aftermarket upgrades — are blurring the lines between bicycles, scooters and motor vehicles.
State and local regulations, many of which were originally written to manage the glut of low-speed rideshare scooters nearly a decade ago, haven’t kept pace, some experts say, and they’ve left city officials scrambling to do more.
The victim in the Washington, D.C., incident was Talib Shakir, who worked in the office of D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser. Police said neither Shakir nor the woman he collided with was wearing a helmet, and that Shakir’s e-scooter could reach speeds up to 55 miles per hour.
A few days later, D.C.’s Metropolitan Police launched a street safety initiative focused on educating e-bike and e-scooter riders about road safety.
In New York City, local leaders held a hearing in August to discuss a slate of new regulations for e-bikes and e-scooters. As of September, at least 28 New Yorkers riding electric devices have died in crashes, the city’s highest-ever total by that point in the year.
A month before the Massachusetts accident, Gov. Maura Healey proposed legislation to establish safety standards and other regulations for e-scooters and e-bikes.
Healey, a Democrat, called existing laws around so-called micromobility devices “unclear and inconsistent,” in a May 2026 statement announcing her bill, which is currently in committee.
“We are seeing too much reckless behavior, more crashes and close calls,” she said, “and too many people, especially pedestrians and young riders, are at risk.”
And after several highly publicized deaths in the Atlanta metro area, including the woman who died after she was thrown from her bike and a teen who died when his e-scooter collided with a tractor-trailer, local officials in surrounding communities have been under pressure to address safety issues.
States including Illinois, Michigan and Pennsylvania have enacted or considered new restrictions this year. The feds have been studying the issue, too: A report released earlier this year from the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission found the number of fatalities from e-scooters and e-bikes has been steadily increasing.

Cost of employer-sponsored health insurance plans rises again, nonpartisan survey finds
The price health insurance companies charge for employer-sponsored plans increased again this year, according to a survey by KFF (krisanapong detraphiphat/Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — The price health insurance companies charge for employer-sponsored plans increased again this year, as did the deductible many people must pay before those plans begin covering most healthcare costs, according to a survey released Thursday by the nonpartisan health organization KFF.
The cost of individual health insurance plans rose to $9,804 on average, while family coverage reached $28,303. Both represented a 5% increase over the last year.
Employees paid about $1,672 for individual coverage, while employers contributed $8,132. People with health insurance for a family of four paid $7,471, with employers providing $20,833.
The amount of money an employee pays toward an individual health insurance plan rose by $232, or 16%, from 2025 to 2026. The price an employee pays for a family health insurance policy increased by $621, or 9%, according to the survey.
“We have been hearing a lot about Affordable Care Act and Medicaid cuts,” KFF President and CEO Drew Altman said in a statement. “Now add a 9% increase in what workers with employer coverage paid toward family premiums in 2026 to the reasons voters are so concerned about their health care costs.”
The national survey looked at the health insurance costs of more than 1,900 employers throughout the country who have at least 10 workers.
The cost of employer-sponsored health insurance plans has steadily gone up for the last 15 years, according to KFF’s data. In 2011, the cost of an individual plan totaled just under $5,500 and family plans cost $15,220 annually.
The average deductible reached $1,995 for single coverage this year, meaning even with health insurance, most employees had to pay a couple thousand dollars out of pocket before their policies kicked in. That’s more than doubled since 2011 when the average annual deductible was $955.
The KFF survey found that 88% of workers with individual coverage had a deductible in 2026.
What types of healthcare coverage people get with the various employer-sponsored health insurance plans varied considerably, sometimes based on the size of their company.
Twenty-seven percent of employers with more than 200 employees, called large firms in the KFF survey, covered the costs of in vitro fertilization, or IVF.
But that fluctuated, with 24% of companies between 200 and 999 workers covering IVF, 38% of companies between 1,000 and 4,999 employees providing coverage and 47% of companies with more than 5,000 workers offering a health insurance plan that covers IVF.
Access to GLP-1 drugs, which can help people manage Type 2 diabetes and lower their weight, also varied based on the size of someone’s employer. Eighteen percent of large firms covered those drugs during 2026, though that was slightly lower than the 19% that covered it during 2025.

When I was pregnant, my ex-husband pinned me against a wall. I was afraid he would kill me.
I survived that violence. I also have a felony conviction. And those two parts of my life cannot be separated.
My ex-husband and I often used methamphetamine together. Our drug use led to countless arguments, and I endured repeated physical and emotional abuse. When I tried to stay sober, he pressured me to use drugs with him.
Once, while I was sober and he had relapsed, he trapped me in the bedroom of our trailer. For hours, he paced back and forth with a bat, screaming in my face and threatening me.
When someone has that much power over your life, saying no doesn’t always feel safe. At times, I believed my choices were to use drugs or face more violence. I made decisions I regret, but I made them while living in fear.
My methamphetamine use eventually led to my arrest and felony conviction.
I understand that I should be held accountable for the crimes I committed. But accountability and understanding are not mutually exclusive. When the court system ignores the circumstances surrounding a crime, it fails to recognize the full story.
In court, I tried to explain how domestic violence had influenced my decisions. But I felt the judge gave little consideration to what I had endured. I believe that if my abuse had been taken seriously, I might have had a better chance to enter a treatment program, get away from my husband and find sobriety sooner.
Today, I celebrate eight years of sobriety and a home free from abuse. I have earned credentials in addiction counseling and peer support. My life is very different from what it was then, but my conviction remains part of my story.
And my experience is not unique.
Missouri Appleseed, a nonprofit advocating for criminal justice reform, has documented the experiences of women whose abuse and coercion contributed to crimes that led to incarceration.
The organization is championing the Missouri Survivors’ Justice Act, which would give survivors a meaningful opportunity to present evidence of domestic violence or coercion during sentencing.
If abuse contributed to someone’s crime, judges should be required to take those circumstances into account when determining an appropriate sentence.
A version of the legislation advanced out of a Missouri House committee earlier this year but did not become law. Advocates plan to renew the effort during the 2027 legislative session.

History Favors Stocks Post-Midterms, But Experts Say Fundamentals Matter More
US equity markets typically rise following midterm elections, but many on Wall Street aren't convinced the outcome matters as much as long-term fundamentals do.
With the US midterm election scheduled for Nov. 3, what to expect afterward is top of mind for many investors.
The S&P 500 has posted an average gain of about 15% in the 12 months following midterm elections since 1950, J.P. Morgan Asset Management said in a note Oct. 7.
That's because getting past elections helps markets refocus on the fundamentals that include corporate earnings, monetary policy and the artificial intelligence spending boom, J.P. Morgan Global Market Strategist Jordan Jackson said.
"In short, history is on the side of investors after midterms," Jackson said. "Rather than trying to trade around the election, investors should stay invested, remain diversified and keep their focus on the longer-term drivers of returns."
The benchmark equity index's return has averaged 5.7% and 12.4% in the three and six months, respectively, following midterm elections since 1974, Charles Schwab said Aug. 18.
"Markets often experience election-related volatility, but history suggests investors are generally better served by staying focused on long-term goals rather than making portfolio decisions based on election outcomes," Charles Schwab Managing Director of Legislative and Regulatory Affairs Michael Townsend said.
Both Jackson and Townsend, however, cautioned against interpreting historical averages as forecasts.
"No statistic should be taken in isolation," Jackson said. "Past midterm cycles have unfolded against very different economic backdrops."
Republicans hold slim majorities in both the US House of Representatives and Senate. At stake in the midterm election are all 435 House of Representative seats and 35 Senate jobs.
The NBC News average of national polls shows majority of Americans prefer a Congress controlled by Democrats. This comes as President Donald Trump's approval ratings have fallen to 36% as of Oct. 22 from 42% at the start of the year amid higher energy prices due to the Iran war, according to The New York Times' daily average of polls.
The eventual congressional control will determine the Trump administration's ability to shape legislation around taxes, government spending and business regulation, Wells Fargo Investment Institute said in a report published Oct. 15.
While that could have implications for certain sectors, it is unlikely to influence the direction of broader equity markets, Wells Fargo wrote.
"Policy changes related to healthcare subsidies, housing affordability, energy, AI and data center investment could have greater impact on the relative performance of specific sectors, rather than altering the direction of the broader market," Wells Fargo said.
If Democrats get control of Congress, some technology companies could face greater scrutiny around competition, data privacy and AI, Morgan Stanley said last month. Energy producers could be subject to a renewed focus on prices, taxes and fossil fuel.

P&G gave investors exactly what they wanted: steady growth. Sales rose 4% in its fiscal first quarter, mostly because people bought more of its products. The unit that makes Tide and P&G's other cleaning products grew 5%. The company also stuck with its full-year outlook.
"The consumer is with us," CFO Andre Schulten told Yahoo Finance on Thursday. In a market searching for safety, that was enough.
Investors are paying up for safety
P&G now costs more than some of the biggest names in tech.

Defendant Jacqueline Fox, who managed the property and owned the LLC that owns the property, initially told the woman that she would be approved to move in.

Zurich American does not get to reclassify a loss as one with a much higher deductible after it had already paid part of the claim, a federal appeals court said in a case involving rain damage to a massive solar farm in Georgia.
“Golfers get mulligans. But in this case, the insurance company does not,” the U.S. 11th Circuit Court of Appeals wrote in its Oct. 22 opinion.
Zurich American had written a builder’s risk policy for First Solar, which was constructing a 200-megawatt solar plant near Warner Robins, in central Georgia, in 2018. Five heavy rain events in 2019 and 2020 left water standing in the former farm field, causing extensive damage to the solar components.
A Zurich adjuster determined that the loss was due to water damage, not flooding, and Zurich sent advance payments totaling $600,000 for the first three rainfall events. The policy allowed a $100,000 per-event deductible for water damage.
But Zurich then reversed course, arguing that the deluges in 2019 and 2020 were actually flood events. In the policy, flood damage carried a much higher deductible—$2.5 million per event. That meant that all of the claimed damage was below the First Solar policy deductible and no payout was due, Zurich argued, as the court explained.
Litigation ensued. After a jury in the U.S. District Court in the Middle District of Georgia found in favor of First Solar, the judge awarded $12.2 million, including prejudgment interest.
Both sides appealed parts of the decision.
A key question was the wording of the policy. Water damage was defined as “all damage caused by water, whatever the source, whether or not driven by wind, other than that otherwise defined as flood or that resulting from a named storm.”
Still, Zurich insisted that it was flooding that swamped the solar farm. First Solar’s team at one point argued that because the property was written as being on normally dry land and at least partly in a Level 3 flood area—with only moderate risk of flooding—it had to be considered water damage.
Even the solar firm’s insurance agent, John Shaw, got involved, urging Zurich and the adjuster to consider the claim to be caused by water, not flooding.
The 11th Circuit appellate court panel upheld the district court on the first three rain event claims, and remanded the case for more deliberations on the two later rainfalls. The appeals court opinion noted that its reading of the policy and the evidence showed that the higher flood deductible actually applied, in this case.
But Zurich had already waived that deductible by paying out on the first three claims as water damage, and by not reserving its rights to change coverage determination, the court decided.
“The central question in this appeal is whether Georgia law permits an insurer in Zurich’s situation to take a mulligan—to receive a do-over after messing up the first time,” 11th Circuit Judge Embry Kidd wrote in the opinion. “Or, under Georgia law, did Zurich’s conduct waive its right to apply the flood deductible after previously applying the water damage deductible?”
The answer is “yes:” Zurich waived its right and hooked its tee shot into the woods. No mulligan.
The court also found that an oddly worded clause in the policy did not require that legal action had to commence within 12 months of the events. “Accordingly, we conclude that the suit against the company provision is not a suit-limitation provision,” the judges wrote.

The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality has shut down its automated electronic filing system after watchdog groups said the agency violated a directive from Gov. Greg Abbott and issued multiple stormwater permits related to data center construction.
The agency said it had suspended specific data center permits identified by the watchdog groups this week. On Wednesday, TCEQ also announced on its website that its electronic filing system “used for automatic authorizations” was being temporarily disabled.
“To ensure all applications are thoroughly reviewed by agency staff to determine if they are related to data centers, applications must be physically provided to TCEQ,” agency spokesman Ryan Vise said in a statement.
The online system, called the State of Texas Environmental Electronic Reporting System, or STEERS, is used for a wide array of permit applications, including those related to air and water pollution. It’s also used for companies to report operational information. The system allows some permits to initially be automatically approved.
The STEERS web portal on Wednesday was inaccessible.
Public Citizen, an advocacy group that’s been fighting data center development along with concerned residents, and FracTracker Alliance, a nonprofit that researches environmental impact from industrial development, identified multiple stormwater permits that the groups said had been approved by TCEQ for large construction projects related to data centers.
Their findings came a month after Abbott told TCEQ to stop issuing “all permits related to data center projects” while other state agencies and the state electric grid operator gathered and checked information about data centers’ proposed water and power use.
The agency’s chaotic messaging and actions along with the shutdown showed the pause wasn’t real until the media and watchdogs scrutinized it, Sam Law, research and communications manager for FracTracker Alliance, wrote in an email. The groups identified other types of permits they said TCEQ had been advancing.
“If our own environmental regulator can’t figure out which permits belong to data centers or have to take down their entire system because of them, it’s a real sign that we need a real moratorium backed by legislation,” Law wrote.
Stormwater permits help regulate water quality impacts from water flowing over a construction site that can have pollutants, according to the agency’s website. Companies submit a “notice of intent” in the online system, which would then get automatically approved.
“In this case, the agency’s rubber stamp worked so well, even the agency had difficulty stopping it,” said Kathryn Guerra, director of Public Citizen’s TCEQ Watchdog Campaign, in a prepared statement. “Texans don’t need another reason to distrust TCEQ, but here it is.”

Most US House races aren’t competitive. What does that mean for how lawmakers govern?
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — Fewer than 5% of U.S. House races are seen by a top political analysis as truly competitive heading into November’s midterm elections, giving relatively few voters the ability to determine which party controls the chamber for the next two years.
The other 414 of 435 House districts are viewed by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report with Amy Walter as at least leaning toward a Democrat or a Republican, as of Oct. 22.
That lack of competition, once a primary election is won, heavily influences which priorities lawmakers pursue in office, according to experts interviewed by States Newsroom. It also means voters in those regions have less ability to hold lawmakers accountable during the general election, especially if those politicians haven’t kept their campaign promises or were embroiled in an ethics scandal.
“For a lot of candidates it’s that primary which is particularly important,” said Zachary Peskowitz, professor of political science at Emory University in Georgia. “And so that obviously creates very different incentives for how they behave in Congress than if they were concerned with the general election.”
There’s evidence the significant number of uncompetitive House races during the general election can lead to “more extreme ideological positions,” he said.
“It can generate a kind of more confrontational style to lawmaking, where your goal is to activate your partisan supporters as opposed to reaching out toward the middle or across the aisle,” Peskowitz said.
While gerrymandering has led to more hyper-partisan House districts, there are other factors as well, including that voters tend to focus more on political party than the specific characteristics and policy proposals of an individual candidate, he said.
Among the lowest in decades
The number of truly competitive House races this year is among the lowest during the last three decades, according to ratings from the Cook Political Report. That’s the case despite the enormous amount of attention paid to which party ultimately will end up with control of the chamber.

It’s easy to catch the marathon bug. Influencers and everyday runners flood social media talking about their training, their accomplishments, and their speedy splits. And when your options range from exciting destination races and multiday challenge events to the coveted World Marathon Majors, it’s easy to get caught up in signing up for 26.2 after 26.2.
But can you run too many marathons?
What does a race calendar that brings out your best performances—while still supporting your recovery and life outside of running—actually look like?
We talked to an exercise physiologist and a sports psychology researcher to find out the physical and mental effects of marathoning and how to determine the number of races per year that keeps you motivated and feeling accomplished without overwhelm or burnout.
How Many Marathons Should You Race in a Year?
It’s absolutely possible to go overboard on marathoning, Janet Hamilton, CSCS, an exercise physiologist and the founder and head coach of Running Strong, tells Runner’s World. Many factors play into the number of races per year that best serves an individual, she explains.
One of the most important to consider? Your overall goal.
“Do you have some sort of a time goal, like you want to qualify for Boston? Or do you just want to be able to say you’ve completed one every month? Those two goals are very different,” she explains.
Racing a marathon at an all-out effort places much more stress on the body than jogging one at your easy pace. Of course, both efforts still require recovery, adds Hamilton. “But if you have a specific performance goal, it behooves you to train with that purpose in mind,” she says.
This means setting aside a full cycle of training to properly base-build, add in speed, gradually taper, and finally, race. To achieve your best result, you can’t rush any part of this process.
Hamilton’s guidance for most runners who want to race well is to aim for a maximum of two, maybe three, marathons per year. “Can you get away with more than that? Sure. Some people complete streaks of marathoning every weekend,” she says. “But that can be really hard on your body, physiologically speaking.”
What Happens to Your Body When You Race Too Often?
Significant physiological changes occur following a long-duration hard-effort exercise bout such as the marathon, explains Hamilton. This can include weakened immune function—part of the reason many runners come down with a postrace cold—elevation of enzymes that indicate cardiac damage, increased levels of the stress hormone cortisol, and a decrease in testosterone levels.
“Generally, your body will come back in balance with a proper recovery cycle,” Hamilton says. But if you never give yourself a break from racing, it becomes much more challenging for you to fully recuperate. “Over time, this takes a toll on your body. Wall Street investors are fleeing stocks at a pace that has Bank of America scrambling to explain what is actually happening, and the real danger may not be the selling itself but where everyone is running for cover.
Wall Street’s love affair with artificial intelligence is running into an uncomfortable reality. After spending much of 2026 piling into AI stocks, investors are discovering that even revolutionary technology has a price ceiling. Rising borrowing costs, enormous data-center spending commitments, and questions about when those investments will pay off have sent traders looking for the exits.
But the selling is spreading far beyond the AI companies that started the trouble. Money managers are unloading stocks across entire sectors, raising the possibility that the market’s next big risk isn’t simply an AI bubble bursting — it’s the rush to escape one.
Bank of America Uncovers a $14.8 Billion Exodus

Jim Cramer called dividend reinvestment plans the place where some big money gets made, but the tax code and the risk of concentration tell a more complicated story about who should actually follow that advice.
A caller asked Jim Cramer something almost every income investor eventually faces during the October 22, 2026 episode of Mad Money: should a brokerage automatically reinvest dividends through a DRIP, or should the cash land in the account so the investor can invest it by hand? Cramer answered: “I am a huge dividend reinvestment plan person. You’ve got to reinvest them. That’s where some big money can be made.”
He has made this case before. In August, Cramer told a caller that his charitable trust must send out its dividends, and he said, “It has really hurt my long-term performance.” For investors still building wealth, the math supports him. The exceptions and the tax bill deserve equal attention.
How a DRIP Puts Every Dividend to Work
A dividend reinvestment plan takes your dividends and uses them to buy more shares of the same stock. Most mutual funds also let shareholders reinvest distributions automatically, according to IRS Publication 550. Most brokerages buy fractional shares, so the whole payout goes back into the position on the payment date.
Each new share then earns its own dividend the next quarter. Take a hypothetical $10,000 position yielding 3%, paid quarterly, with a share price that never moves. An investor who takes the cash collects $9,000 over 30 years and still owns a $10,000 position. Reinvesting every payout grows the position to about $24,514, generating roughly $735 a year in dividends, compared with the $300 the cash recipient still receives. Price gains or dividend raises widen that gap.
On the same episode, Cramer described sending small checks to the Fidelity Magellan Fund for decades: “The power of compounding. I never touched it.”
When Taking the Cash Makes More Sense
Retirees living on portfolio income are the clearest case. If dividends pay for groceries and property taxes, reinvesting them only forces share sales later to raise the same money. Collecting the payout is the plan working as designed. Cramer still wants retirees to keep a mix of assets: “People should always be investing for growth and some for dividend and then some for bonds.”
Manual redeployment also suits investors who want control. A DRIP keeps buying whatever paid the dividend, which can slowly concentrate a portfolio in its biggest payers. Cramer learned the cost of concentration at Goldman Sachs (NYSE:GS | GS Price Prediction), remembering that “those who owned nothing but oil stocks, including yours truly” took heavy losses. Collecting dividends lets you send them to an underweight holding or a new idea.
Reinvested Dividends Still Trigger a Tax Bill
In a taxable account, the IRS taxes reinvested dividends in the year they are paid. If you use dividends to buy more stock at fair market value, “you must still report the dividends as income.” If the plan offers shares at a discount, you report the fair market value of the additional stock on the dividend payment date as dividend income. The tax code says the dividend portion of a distribution “shall be included in gross income” (26 U.S.C. § 301(c)(1)). That tax has to come from cash you never actually received.

"When I was CEO at Google, we set the revenue growth record. They smashed it more than twice the speed as we did," Schmidt told Nicolai Tangen, head of Norway's sovereign wealth fund, on the In Good Company podcast.
"That's real growth there. It's not fake. It's real money with real customers who are paying for something useful in their eyes."
Schmidt, who led Google, now part of Alphabet Inc., from 2001 to 2011, did not specify how he calculated the comparison.

Anthropic's Growth Comes With Enormous Costs

The company also told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis, although revenue growth slowed after more than doubling between the first and second quarters.

Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on computing and infrastructure during those six months and has committed at least $518 billion over a decade.

"If you define losing as users, the vast majority of the world will use the free Chinese models rather than the more expensive Western models," he said.

Procter & Gamble (PG -2.12%) just had its best day in more than six years, with the stock jumping 5.6% on Thursday after the company delivered a surprisingly strong fiscal first quarter in a challenging environment.
During a time when many of its customers are struggling with inflation and a high cost of living, the household products giant reported 4% organic sales growth. That performance also represents a significant bounce from flat organic sales growth in the previous quarter, which helps explain why the stock had its best day since the market started soaring in the recovery from the pandemic crash in March 2020.
Organic volume was up 2.4%, and the company delivered strong results in beauty, fabric, and home care. Overall revenue rose 4% to $23.3 billion, which topped estimates at $22.8 billion.
Despite strong organic sales growth, core gross margin fell by 150 basis points, primarily due to higher commodity costs, reflecting higher oil prices than a year ago. Nonetheless, its productivity savings program helped improve selling, general, and administrative margins, and operating margin fell 70 basis points to 25.5%.
On the bottom line, the company reported core earnings per share of $2.00, up from $1.99 in the quarter a year ago, and ahead of the consensus at $1.89.
Why the stock soared on the news
P&G maintained its full-year core EPS guidance of $6.89-$7.11, and the company expects headwinds from higher commodity costs and oil prices to increase over the rest of the year.
Nonetheless, the company seemed to reverse earlier concerns about slumping growth, doing so at a time when many consumer brands are struggling. Four percent organic growth is outstanding for any mature consumer staples business, and that's the figure investors should focus on.
The news also came on a day when tech stocks plunged, and the sell-off may have beckoned more investors to rotate into P&G, which is seen as one of the most rock-solid, defensive stocks on the market.

I’ve always been more of an anaerobic athlete, meaning I love shorter, faster running and strength workouts. In fact, I love strength so much that even during my first marathon training block, I enthusiastically committed to three heavy lifts a week.
While strength training prevents injuries, makes you more durable, and can even boost your running economy, says Des Clarke, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Phoenix, I often spent evenings in the gym lifting weights instead of allowing my body to recover from 40-mile weeks.
As I started training for a half marathon for the second time, I decided to put more of an emphasis on mileage. I didn’t want to nix strength from my schedule entirely, but I had to figure out how to dial back my time with the weights and increase my running time in a safe, balanced way.
Doing so helped me run a 1:46:50 half marathon on a majorly hilly course. Here’s what I did to get there so you can strike a better balance, too.
How I Increased My Mileage Safely Without Sacrificing Strength
For anyone running half marathons and marathons (especially someone who’s newer to longer distances like I am), higher mileage weeks give you the base you need to run longer and faster.
“If you want to get better at running, it is true that to a point, you need to run more,” says Clarke. “You’re building the aerobic capacity, strength, and durability that you need to run those distances without getting injured.” That looks like building volume incrementally over time, she says.
Before I started half marathon training, I was running at least two times each week for about eight months. I was pretty consistent, but knew I could afford to add more miles. So before starting my plan, I added another day of running to my schedule, and then when I kicked off the first week, I tackled four days a week of running.
I also added some more miles to my midweek runs. Last training cycle, I usually opted for four-milers, but this time, I bumped it up to five or six miles.
Clarke typically recommends repeating the same weekly mileage for two to three weeks in a row to make sure an athlete has adapted to that particular load before increasing again. I did this during several weeks of my plan.
In that same vein, it’s useful to take a deload week every three weeks or so to better absorb training gains, Clarke says. This involves scaling back your mileage by around 10 to 20 percent before returning to your typical volume. My training plan also included these, allowing me recovery time while pushing mileage.
To balance this increase in mileage, I dropped to two lifting days per week instead of three, cutting down on volume (and consequently my overall time spent in the gym), which Clarke recommends. Last year during marathon training, I spent three days a week lifting weights for about an hour or more. This training cycle, I’ve spent 30 to 45 minutes lifting weights one to two times a week. I split up my usual hour-long routine into two separate days and alternated between them.

Google Cloud's backlog just crossed $500 billion while free cash flow turned negative for the first time ever, and Wednesday's earnings report will reveal whether Alphabet's historic spending spree is pulling ahead of its own ability to pay for it.
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL | GOOGL Price Prediction, NASDAQ:GOOG) reports third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Google Cloud’s backlog stands at $514 billion, and 2026 CapEx guidance runs $195 billion to $205 billion. This report shows which one is growing faster.
Record Cloud Growth Meets Negative Free Cash Flow
Last quarter, revenue rose 24.2% to $119.80 billion, ahead of the $116.91 billion consensus. Google Cloud led again. Revenue there rose 82% to $24.77 billion, speeding up from 63% in Q1 and 34% a year ago, while Cloud operating margin expanded to 35.6% from 20.7%.
Costs grew just as fast. CapEx rose 100% to $44.92 billion, free cash flow came in at negative $5.86 billion — the first time ever — and management raised its 2026 CapEx range from $180 billion to $190 billion. To pay for it, Alphabet raised about $70 billion in equity and debt and suspended buybacks.
Reported EPS of $9.11 included a $99.03 billion equity securities gain, yet shares fell 6.89% on the day of the report. GOOG closed Friday at $317.28, down 5.83% over the past week.
Consensus Calls for Nearly 25% Revenue Growth
The full-year EPS figure includes the first half’s equity gains, which makes the quarterly estimate the cleaner gauge of operating profit.
Backlog Conversion and Margins Will Set the Tone
My first focus will be the backlog. It rose by more than $50 billion sequentially last quarter, and management expects to recognize just over 50% of it within 24 months. Sundar Pichai said in July, “We are still in a supply-constrained environment.”
Margins come next. Alphabet planned to lean on third-party capacity in Q3 as a bridge, which management said would create “modest margin pressure,” on top of Wiz integration costs and rising depreciation. You should compare Cloud margin against 35.6% and consolidated operating margin against 34%.
On spending, any change to the 2026 range matters, as does early color on 2027, when management expects CapEx to “increase significantly.” TPU system sales add another variable. That revenue ramps as Alphabet leaves 2026, with the “vast majority” arriving in 2027.
All that CapEx has to be powered, cooled, and connected by somebody, which is the entire point of a free report we put together on seven AI infrastructure suppliers that aren’t the chipmakers: you can grab it here.
Search still has to fund the expansion. Revenue there grew 17% to $63.3 billion, and AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly users. A court has already rejected a forced breakup of Google’s ad-tech business, so any detail on the remaining behavioral remedies could also move opinion.
A $514 Billion Backlog Has to Turn Into Cash
Alphabet beat estimates in all 8 of its last reports. Even so, the stock’s moves on report day ranged from a 9.97% gain to a 6.89% drop, and the market now cares most about how efficiently that capital gets spent. If the backlog turns into revenue fast enough to steady free cash flow while CapEx keeps rising, the spending case gets easier to defend heading into a greater 2027.
